period: Scholars commonly place it in the second half of the first millennium BCE, after the oldest prose Upanishads; dating is uncertain
summary: A dialogue in which the boy Nachiketa, sent to the realm of Death, asks Yama what happens after death and learns about the undying Self.
whyRead: Katha is the most story-driven of the principal Upanishads and one of the most quoted. Its image of the self as a chariot's rider, its choice between the good and the pleasant, and its verses on the undying Self reappear almost word for word in the Bhagavad Gita.
story: Nachiketa's father performs a sacrifice in which he gives away everything, yet offers only worn-out cows. When the boy persists in asking to whom he himself will be given, the father angrily says, 'to Death'. Nachiketa goes to Yama's house and waits three nights unfed, so Yama grants him three boons. The third is to know whether a person exists after death; Yama tries to dissuade him with offers of wealth and long life, but Nachiketa refuses them all, and Yama teaches him about the Self.
questions: Why choose the good over the pleasant?
How are mind, senses and Self related?

keyTeachings.title: The good and the pleasant
keyTeachings.text: Yama distinguishes shreyas, what is truly good, from preyas, what is merely pleasant. The wise choose the good; Nachiketa's refusal of Yama's gifts shows this choice.

keyTeachings.title: The Self is unborn and undying
keyTeachings.text: The Self is not born and does not die; it is not slain when the body is slain. These verses are closely paralleled in Gita 2.19–20.

keyTeachings.title: The chariot image
keyTeachings.text: The Self is the rider, the body the chariot, the intellect (buddhi) the charioteer, the mind the reins and the senses the horses. Freedom depends on a discerning intellect guiding a controlled mind.

keyTeachings.title: Not reached by learning alone
keyTeachings.text: The Self is said not to be attained by instruction, intellect or much learning, but by the one whom it chooses, a verse also found in the Mundaka Upanishad.

keyTeachings.title: The inverted tree
keyTeachings.text: The world is pictured as an eternal asvattha tree with roots above and branches below, an image taken up in Gita 15.1.

structure.note: Frame story and the three boons
